description: The Water Conflict Chronology of the Pacific Institute is a long-running database of incidents in which water was a trigger, a casualty or a weapon of violence, compiled and curated for more than three decades as the core of its Water and Peace Initiative. Entries run from ancient disputes such as Lagash and Umma around 2500 BC to current events, and each gives a short description, date, location and category; the institute reports 420 water conflict events recorded in 2024 alone, a 20 percent rise on 2023 and 78 percent on 2022. Cases include dams torn down or targeted, wells dried up or poisoned, aqueducts breached, rivers diverted, and clashes over access between farmers and pastoralists. Events can be explored on a public map and in a chronological list, free of charge; the institute calls it the most complete open-source database of its kind, but no licence text or bulk download was found on the pages read, and a peer-reviewed paper describes its definitions and trends. Caveats: entries are compiled from media and published sources so coverage reflects reporting, classifications are the institute's, and descriptions are short, with few technical details on the infrastructure damaged. Simulation uses: building threat scenarios for deliberate attacks on water systems, frequency baselines for security risk in water infrastructure models, and case selection for studies of conflict-driven outages. Related records: the England reservoir flood extents (data-england-reservoir-flood-extents) as an example of consequence data for dam failure scenarios.
